# The French-speaking market: prospecting France, Belgium, Switzerland and Quebec

Research pass of 2026-10-29 for the BeReach skill pack. Scope: how a first LinkedIn message (and its email cousin)
should be written for French-speaking B2B readers. Address form (vous or tu) by sector, formality, length and
tone, what French buyers dislike, who the French experts are (and which of them sell something), the studies on
French B2B buyers, LinkedIn usage figures, the rules of the CNIL and of the Belgian, Swiss and Canadian regulators,
and worked examples of good and bad first messages.

Files: `sources.md` (every URL, read in full or only in summary), `evidence.md` (every claim with its rating).

What this folder does NOT repeat (read those first):

- `../linkedin-messages/README.md` section 7: vous by default, "Bonjour Prénom,", space before "?" and "!".
- `../cold-email/README.md` sections 2 and 8: the CNIL email rules, the October 2026 CNIL note on guessed work
  addresses, the KASPR fine, the UK and German rules.
- `../personas/README.md` ("Addressing the reader formally or informally") and `../voice/README.md` section 8:
  Brown and Gilman, Clyne, Norrby and Warren, the German du/Sie study. Copy the user's own address form first.

This folder adds the parts those leave thin: the evidence behind the tu/vous rule per sector and per country, the
French buyer studies, the cultural frameworks, the legal position of a LinkedIn message (as opposed to an email),
Belgium, Switzerland and Quebec, and written examples.

## Ratings

| Rating | Means |
|---|---|
| Measured | A study or large dataset with a stated method (sample, how it was counted) |
| Survey | People asked about themselves, with a stated sample |
| Practice | Experienced practitioners or official style bodies, no measurement |
| Vendor | A seller's own data or claims about its own users or market |
| Untraced | Repeated, but no primary source found, or the source does not say it |

Regulator texts (CNIL, BAKOM, CRTC) are quoted as what the regulator says; they are rated Practice for "how it will
be enforced" and are not legal advice.

## Summary table

| # | Finding | Rating | Use in a message |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | No published test compares tu and vous on B2B reply rates, in any French-speaking market | (absence, checked) | The tu/vous choice is a judgment, not a measured lever. Default vous, mirror on reply |
| 2 | In consumer experiments, informal address helps "warm" brands and formal address helps "competent" ones (6 experiments, several languages) | Measured (consumer, not B2B) | A B2B seller selling expertise to a stranger is in the "competent" case: vous |
| 3 | Inside French companies tu is common with the boss (about 63% private vs 43% public sector, 70% of men vs 49% of women, Alber; a 2013 TNS Sofres "56%" is repeated but its source was not found) | Survey (Alber, via article); Untraced (TNS) | Workplace tu among colleagues does not transfer to a stranger selling something |
| 4 | Quebec: tu at a first meeting is "far more common" than in other French-speaking regions, yet the official body still says vous at first contact is the safer choice | Practice (OQLF, official) | Quebec: vous in message 1, switch fast if they write tu |
| 5 | Switzerland (Romandie): both forms coexist and the unwritten rule is to wait for the manager to propose tu; tech and start-ups use tu "quasi-universellement"; private banks and law firms keep vous, at least with senior people | Practice (weak, anonymous guide) | Same as France, with a stronger "vous" in banking and law |
| 6 | France is "principles-first": readers want the reason before the proposal (Meyer) | Practice (INSEAD professor's model from interviews and teaching, not a measured study) | One clause of why before the ask; no bare "can we talk?" |
| 7 | France scores 86 on uncertainty avoidance and 68 on power distance (Hofstede tool) | Measured (old IBM-based scores, updated tool) | No hype, no unprovable claims; write to the reader's level, respect titles in traditional sectors |
| 8 | French B2B buyers research alone for about 12 months of a 17-month journey before the first sales contact; committees of about 12 | Survey (205 decision makers, media group) | A first message meets someone already informed: offer a useful angle, not a product tour |
| 9 | 45% of French B2B decision makers had answered a social-network approach from a stranger; 20% had bought after one (2020) | Survey (650, agency plus La Poste) | Cold LinkedIn outreach works on a minority, as everywhere |
| 10 | LinkedIn France: about 37 to 40 million registered or addressable accounts in 2026; monthly active users unknown (one vendor estimate 14 million) | Vendor or platform data, registered not active | Never quote a member count as an audience |
| 11 | CNIL: B2B electronic prospecting needs no prior consent if the message relates to the person's job, tells them where their data came from and why, and lets them refuse simply | Official (CNIL, page dated 10 June 2026) | Make the first message say why them and offer an easy "no" |
| 12 | Collecting from a professional network goes beyond reasonable expectations when the member restricted the data's visibility (KASPR, EUR 240,000, Dec 2024) | Official decision | Use only what the person shows publicly; never hidden contact data |
| 13 | Whether French e-prospecting law covers LinkedIn messages is not settled by any text found; Canada's regulator says LinkedIn messaging IS covered by its anti-spam law | Official (Canada); untraced (France) | Write every first message as if the email rules apply: identity, relevance, origin, opt-out |
| 14 | Switzerland: mass advertising by telecom needs consent, B2B included; individual one-to-one messages are probably outside the "mass" rule | Official (mass rule); untraced (individual) | Keep Swiss outreach individual and relevant |

## 1. What the French buyer studies actually say

There are few. Most "French B2B buyer" figures online are vendor blog numbers with no method. The three with a
stated sample:

### Infopro Digital, "Buyer Journey 2026" (via The Media Leader, 12 October 2026)

- 205 decision makers who took part in a purchase over EUR 25,000. Method and fieldwork dates not given on the page
  read (summary only; the report itself was not found).
- France against a US/UK benchmark: journey 17 months (11), research alone before the first sales contact 12 months
  (7), buying committee 12 people (10), shortlist 5 suppliers (4), 20 interactions with the winning supplier (18).
- 33% of committees that had ranked suppliers before the first contact changed their preferred supplier after
  talking to sales. So the sales conversation still moves decisions.
- Channels used to build the shortlist (separate Infopro 2026 barometer): word of mouth 53%, supplier website 46%,
  specialist press 44%, events 43%, social networks 34%.
- 63% call AI assistants important in supplier research.
- Rating: Survey. Infopro is a B2B media and events group, so it has an interest in "buyers read media first".

What it means for a first message: the reader is likely already informed and is part of a group. A message that
helps them think (a question, a comparison, a peer's experience) fits; a product introduction does not.

### Intuiti and La Poste Solutions Business, "Baromètre Social Selling France 2020"

- 650 B2B decision makers, February to April 2020, third edition. Read through the Blog du Modérateur write-up
  (summary only).
- 84.8% use LinkedIn for work. 45% had answered a sales approach from a stranger on social networks (rising with
  company size). 20% had bought after such an approach (73% of those purchases under EUR 10,000). 37% had bought
  after discovering content. Only 40% think companies share relevant content.
- Rating: Survey, sellers of social selling services (an agency and La Poste's B2B arm).

### Ifop for Notify, consumer solicitation (published 18 April 2025)

- 86% find commercial solicitation intrusive, 65% no longer pay attention, 63% would boycott a brand that contacts
  them without permission. Sample size not stated in the article read.
- It is about consumers and phone or text marketing, not B2B. Quote it only as mood: the French public is tired of
  unsolicited selling, and French professionals are the same people.

### What was looked for and not found

- A French survey of decision makers on LinkedIn messages they dislike (OpinionWay, Ifop, Ipsos, Harris): none found.
- A vendor dataset of French-language LinkedIn messages with reply rates by length or address form: none published
  with a method. Waalaxy publishes French-market advice and global numbers (for example 64 million campaigns: 34.3%
  acceptance without a note against 32.3% with one), but not split by language.
- An A/B test of tu against vous: none, from any vendor or researcher.

The caveat matters: DataReportal says plainly that LinkedIn's numbers are registered members, may include duplicate
or inactive accounts, and are not active users. A French member count above the adult working population is a sign
of that. Nobody outside LinkedIn knows how many French members read their messages each month.

Usage in practice: a "Visibrain analysis of 430,000 French-language posts (April 2024 to April 2025)" finding
recruitment the most discussed topic was seen only in a search summary; no source page was kept and the Blog du
Modérateur 2025 study read (Heaven with Influence Metrics) does not mention it (Untraced). Inboxes have not been
measured either.

## 3. Cultural frameworks

### Erin Meyer, The Culture Map (INSEAD)

- Eight scales built from her work with executives. On "persuading", France is principles-first: people "want to
  understand the reasoning behind a proposal before acting", a habit she traces to French schooling and Descartes.
  Her advice: "provide background principles and welcome debate", explain the why, not just the how (erinmeyer.com,
  read in full).
- Rating: Practice. Meyer's positions come from interviews and her teaching, not a published measured study.
- For a message: an applications-first English message ("Can we talk Tuesday?") reads abrupt in French. Put one
  clause of reasoning before the ask: why this topic, why now, why them. One clause, not a paragraph: principles
  first does not mean long.
- Not verified here: where Meyer places France on the "communicating" (low or high context) and "leading" scales.
  Secondary sources repeat that France is fairly high context and hierarchical; the primary page was not read.

### Geert Hofstede, cultural dimensions (current Culture Factor tool)

- France: power distance 68, individualism 74, motivation towards achievement 43, uncertainty avoidance 86,
  long-term orientation 60, indulgence 48 (tool page read; the individualism value has changed over editions,
  older tables say 71).
- Rating: Measured at origin (IBM employee surveys, later replications), but scores are national averages and decades
  old. Use as a hint, never as a rule about one reader.
- For a message: high uncertainty avoidance means unsupported claims ("le meilleur outil du marché", "x10 sur vos
  ventes") cost trust; precise, checkable facts help. Fairly high power distance means titles and hierarchy are
  noticed: a junior seller writing "tu" to a director of a traditional firm breaks a rule the reader feels.
  Both are inferences from the scores (Practice), not measured on messages.

### OQLF (Office québécois de la langue française), the official guide on vous and tu

- "En général, on vouvoie les personnes qu'on rencontre pour la première fois." Even when a first contact is
  friendly, keeping vous until the question comes up is the cautious choice. Spontaneous tu is usual in workplaces,
  clubs and associations. The older or higher-ranked person proposes the switch.
- The same body notes tu at a first meeting is far more common in Quebec than in other French-speaking regions.
- Rating: Practice (official language authority). Read in full.

### Address forms in research

- Lenoir, ERIM PhD thesis, Erasmus University, 2015 (author name from the file; French summary read in full): six
  experiments, several languages. Informal address is preferred and works better for brands perceived as warm,
  formal address for brands perceived as competent. Consumer contexts (advertising, services), not B2B. Measured.
- Clyne, Norrby and Warren (2009), already in `../voice/README.md`: in French workplaces vous is the default with
  strangers and in hierarchy; the hard part is the switch.
- French workplace surveys: a Bruneau / TNS Sofres 2013 figure (604 employees, 56% use tu with their direct boss,
  64% of managers) appears only in search summaries; the article cited for it does not carry it (Untraced).
  Sociologist Alex Alber, via Welcome to the Jungle (article read): about 63% in the
  private sector against 43% in the public sector, 70% of men against 49% of women. These are colleagues inside one
  company, not a seller writing to a stranger.

## 4. Vous or tu, by market and sector

No measurement decides this. The table below is the consensus of the practitioner and official sources read
(Waalaxy, Overloop, Origami, the Swiss guide, the OQLF), combined with the warm/competent result above. It is a
starting default for a persona card, to be overridden by (a) how the user writes and (b) how the prospect writes.

| Reader | First message | Why |
|---|---|---|
| Start-up founders, tech and SaaS teams, growth and marketing people under about 40, agencies, creative trades | vous + first name is safe; tu acceptable if the reader posts in tu or the user always writes tu | Sector norm is tu inside; every vendor source allows tu here |
| Tech in large groups (CIO, IT director, CTO of a corporate) | vous | The company culture, not the job, decides |
| Traditional industry, manufacturing, logistics, construction | vous | Hierarchy and age; tu reads as a salesman's trick |
| Finance (CFO, DAF, banking, insurance, private banks) | vous | Formal sector; Swiss guide names private banks explicitly |
| Legal, notaries, accounting firms, consulting partners | vous | Formal professions; Maître for lawyers and notaries only in letters, not needed on LinkedIn |
| Real estate: asset managers, investors, property companies | vous | Finance-adjacent and senior |
| Real estate: agencies, brokers, network agents (independent agents) | vous in message 1; many will answer in tu, then follow | Sales culture, informal among peers, but a stranger selling to them is still a stranger |
| Public sector, hospitals, education, elected officials | vous, always | Most formal; tu use at work is lowest in the public sector (Alber survey) |
| Healthcare professionals (doctors, pharmacists) | vous, "Docteur" if writing formally | Status matters |
| Quebec, any sector | vous in message 1, switch at the first tu | OQLF: vous at first contact, but tu comes fast |
| Belgium (French-speaking) | vous | No reliable source says Belgium is more informal in business; sources contradict each other |
| Switzerland (Romandie) | vous | Wait for the other side to propose tu (Swiss guide); vous until then |

Rules that hold across all rows:

1. **Mirror.** If the reader answers in tu, switch to tu. If they answer in vous after your tu, go back to vous at
   once. Never switch back from tu to vous on your own.
2. **"Vous" with the first name is the normal modern form.** "Bonjour Marie, ... vous ..." is standard in French
   LinkedIn and email prospecting (every template set read uses it). Swiss Romandie uses "vous + prénom" heavily.
   "Bonjour Madame Dupont" is more formal: right for senior readers in finance, law, private banking or the public
   sector, stiff for everyone else. "Madame, Monsieur" is for when the name is unknown, which never happens on
   LinkedIn.
3. **Never mix in one message.** "Salut Marie, ... vous" is the commonest bad draft.
4. **Tu with "Salut" and an emoji is a register, not a pronoun.** If tu is chosen, keep everything else in the same
   register as the user's own writing; tu does not license a hype tone.
5. **A tu in a sequence is permanent.** The follow-ups must keep it.

## 5. Greeting, sign-off and typography

| Item | Use | Avoid | Rating |
|---|---|---|---|
| Greeting | "Bonjour Prénom," | "Hello Prénom" outside start-ups; "Cher Monsieur"; "Madame, Monsieur" when the name is known; no greeting at all | Practice; 81% of over 1,000 employees like to be greeted by first name (Livecareer, 2023, method not given): Survey, weak |
| Opening filler | Get to the reason in sentence one | "J'espère que vous allez bien", "Je me permets de vous contacter", "Je suis X de la société Y" as first words | Practice (every French template critique read) |
| Sign-off on LinkedIn | First name, or "Bonne journée," then first name | "Cordialement" (reads as an email), "Bien à vous" is fine in Belgium and email, "Veuillez agréer" never | Practice |
| Sign-off in email | "Bonne journée," or "Belle journée," or "Bien à vous," then name and company | "Cordialement" alone is acceptable but cold | Practice |
| Punctuation | A space before ? ! : ; (a non-breaking or narrow non-breaking space in output); « guillemets » with inner spaces | English spacing ("vous?"), straight English quotes in a French sentence | Practice (French typography norms) |
| Numbers | "12 000", "3,5 %", "15 h" | "12,000", "3.5%", "3pm" | Practice |
| English words | Sector jargon the reader uses (SaaS, pipeline, lead) | Translated English idioms ("Quick question" as "Petite question rapide", "Hope this finds you well", "Ça vous parle ?" as a CTA everywhere) | Practice; Origami and others warn that one machine-translated phrase damages credibility (Vendor) |

On the subject line (email only): `../cold-email/README.md` section 8 already covers it.

## 6. Length and structure in French

- French text runs longer than the English it translates. The localization trade commonly says 15 to 25% longer;
  no primary measurement was found (Untraced). Overloop's "a French cold email is naturally 20 to 30 words longer
  than its US equivalent" cites nothing; its own length table contains only "to measure" cells (Untraced).
- Overloop's other French claims (median French reply rate 4.9% on 50K emails; "62% of managers find cold email
  intrusive, IFOP"; email-only 3.8% against multichannel 6.1% to 8.4% on 200 campaigns) state no method (Vendor,
  near-untraced). Not to be quoted.
- LinkedIn's own line that InMails under 400 characters do best is in `../linkedin-messages/evidence.md` (platform
  claim, no method). Waalaxy's "under 300 characters get 5% more replies" cites nothing.
- Practical rule for French LinkedIn first messages: 2 to 4 sentences, about 300 to 500 characters. Cut ideas, never
  compress grammar into telegraphic fragments: a verbless French fragment ("Deux ans dans la mesure de l'air.")
  reads even colder than in English.
- Structure that fits "principles first" without length: (1) why them, in one sentence that links a fact to a reason;
  (2) one sentence of substance (the problem others in their seat have, or a result for a peer); (3) a low-pressure
  question of interest. The same skeleton as `../linkedin-messages/README.md`, with the reason made explicit.

## 7. What French buyers dislike (and how strong the evidence is)

| Dislike | Evidence | Rating |
|---|---|---|
| A meeting request in the first message ("15 minutes cette semaine ?") | Meeting asks reply 44% less in 85M emails (global, see `../linkedin-messages`); Origami calls "let's jump on a call" an American CTA that fails in France | Measured (vendor, global) plus Vendor practice |
| Familiarity from a stranger: "Salut", tu, emoji, "ton profil m'a interpellé" to a senior or traditional reader | Lenoir (competence wants formal); OQLF (vous at first contact); every French vendor guide | Measured (consumer) plus Practice |
| Machine-translated or anglicised French | Origami, Overloop; no data | Practice / Vendor |
| Hype, superlatives, guaranteed results | Inferred from uncertainty avoidance 86 and Meyer's principles-first; no message-level study | Practice (inference) |
| Flattery that proves nothing ("votre parcours impressionnant") | Waalaxy claims flattering messages reply 17% more, citing "internal LinkedIn data" with no link: the opposite claim, and untraced | Untraced either way: do not flatter, do not rely on it |
| Being asked "Qui est en charge de X chez vous ?" by someone who did not look | Practice | Practice |
| Pitch in the connection note | A La Growth Machine test (31% acceptance with no note, 29% with a sales note, 32% with a vague note) is quoted in search summaries but is not on the page cited; Waalaxy's 64M campaigns: 34.3% without a note against 32.3% with one | Untraced (LGM); Vendor (Waalaxy) |
| Writing in English to a French reader outside international roles | "Prospects outside Paris may not be comfortable in English" (vendor blogs); no data | Practice |
| In Belgium, writing French to a Dutch-speaking reader (or the reverse) | Practice; check the profile language | Practice |

## 8. The law: what a first message must carry

This section adds to `../cold-email/README.md` and is not legal advice.

### France

- **The B2B rule, current CNIL wording** (page "Communications par voie électronique aux prospects et clients", dated
  10 June 2026, read in full): prior consent is not systematically required for B2B prospecting if the message is
  "en lien avec l'activité professionnelle de la personne contactée", the person "est informée de l'origine de ses
  données et de la finalité du message", and "elle peut s'opposer simplement à la réception de nouvelles
  sollicitations". The CNIL recommends a suppression list ("liste repoussoir"). The rules cover "courriel, SMS, MMS,
  automates d'appel et autres technologies"; social network messaging is not named.
- **The statute.** CPCE article L34-5 forbids hiding the identity of the person on whose behalf the message is sent
  and using a subject unrelated to the offer (read only in legal summaries). The LCEN definition of "courrier
  électronique" is broad: any text, voice, sound or image message sent over a public network and stored until the
  recipient fetches it. Whether a LinkedIn private message falls under it has not been ruled on in any text found.
  Treat it as covered.
- **Reusing public data for prospecting** (CNIL recommendations, June 2024, use-case sheet 2, read in full):
  - Public data stays personal data. B2B electronic prospecting of people "sollicitées au titre de leur activité
    professionnelle spécifique" can rest on legitimate interest, if it fits their reasonable expectations.
  - Expectations depend on the source site, its terms (if they forbid collection for prospecting, it falls outside
    expectations), the link between the data and the offer (a cybersecurity training body prospecting DPOs whose
    details the CNIL publishes as open data is the CNIL's own example of a good fit), and the kind of data (job and location are expected; interests, feelings and
    social life profiling are not). Content on a professional network is "a priori" not personal content.
  - Information must reach the person individually, "au plus tard lors de la première prise de contact" and within
    one month of collection, and must name the source (the website names where known).
  - People who objected, or who sit on opposition lists, must not be contacted.
- **KASPR** (SAN-2024-020, 5 December 2024, EUR 240,000, CNIL page read in full): a browser extension that revealed
  LinkedIn members' contact details. Collecting details members had restricted to their first or second degree
  "excédait ce à quoi pouvaient raisonnablement s'attendre" members of a professional network. Also: five-year
  retention reset at each job change, notice in English only, access requests answered without the source information held.
- **Nestor** (SAN-2020-018, 8 December 2020, EUR 20,000): prospecting emails without consent to people who were not
  customers (653,033 people, some of whose data was collected on the internet; Maddyness, read in summary). The CNIL
  2024 sheet (footnote 14) describes Nestor as a company exploiting professional social network data and cites the
  decision for the point that a data broker passing individuals' contact details on for e-prospecting needs their
  prior consent. Whether the recipients were treated as consumers or professionals was not checked in the decision.
- **Guessed work addresses** (CNIL, 16 October 2026): see `../cold-email/README.md`.
- **Phone**: secondary sources report that consent became the rule for consumer cold calls in August 2026 while
  professionals keep a right to object. Not checked against the official text; outside this skill's scope.

What this means for the words of a French first message, with no lawyer in the loop:

1. Say who you are and for which company, in the message or the visible profile.
2. Say why them, in terms of their job (this is both the CNIL relevance condition and the best copy practice).
3. Say where you saw them when it is not obvious ("J'ai vu votre intervention sur ...", "Vous avez commenté ...").
   This covers the "origin of the data" condition in plain words.
4. Offer an easy no: "Si ce n'est pas un sujet pour vous, dites-le-moi simplement et je n'insiste pas." Then honour
   it: never follow up after a no, and keep the person on the user's do-not-contact list.
5. Use only what the person shows publicly on the profile or their posts. Never contact details they hid.

### Belgium

- Electronic advertising is consent-based (Royal Decree of 4 April 2003, now in the Code of Economic Law, articles
  VI.110 and following, per the Belgian data protection authority). The B2B exemption as read by a Belgian law firm
  (Younity, 2017, summary): no opt-in is needed for emails to legal entities "to the extent that the contact details
  are not linked to an individual", for example info@. A named work address is therefore not covered.
- Rating: Practice (one law firm's reading; the decree text was not read). Practical consequence: cold email to a
  named Belgian person is riskier than in France; a LinkedIn message carrying the five elements above is the safer
  first contact. GDPR information and objection duties apply as in France.

### Switzerland

- Unfair Competition Act article 3(1)(o): sending mass advertising by telecom without prior consent, without the
  correct sender, or without an easy free refusal is unfair (BAKOM page, 2 July 2021, read in full; rule in force
  since 1 April 2007). Secondary sources and slides say B2B and B2C are treated alike.
- The rule targets "mass" advertising. Whether one individually written message counts was not settled in any source
  found (Untraced; commentators lean "not mass"). The revised data protection act (in force September 2023) still
  applies to the data.
- Practice: keep Swiss outreach one-to-one and job-relevant, name the sender, offer the easy no.

### Quebec (and Canada)

- Canada's Anti-Spam Legislation (CASL / LCAP) covers commercial electronic messages to "electronic addresses". The
  CRTC FAQ, as quoted by search results (the page itself returned 403), says messages sent through social media
  messaging such as LinkedIn messaging count; public posts do not.
- Implied consent can come from conspicuous publication: the address was published without a "no solicitation"
  statement and the message relates to the person's role or business (CRTC infographic, via law firm summaries).
  A regulation exempts some platform messages from consent if they identify the sender and offer an unsubscribe
  mechanism, which platforms rarely support. The sender carries the burden of proof. Rating: Official, read in
  summary.
- Quebec's own privacy law (Law 25) was not researched here.
- Practice: the same five elements, plus a clear "dites-moi si vous préférez que je ne vous écrive plus".

## 9. Experts and sources: who they are and what they sell

No independent French researcher on cold outreach was found. The French-language field is written almost entirely by
tool vendors. Each is useful for practice, none for numbers.

| Name | Who | Sells | Worth reading for |
|---|---|---|---|
| CNIL | French data protection authority | Nothing | The rules; the 2024 reuse sheet is the most detailed text on prospecting from public profiles |
| OQLF | Quebec's official language office | Nothing | Address forms and letter conventions, Quebec usage |
| Erin Meyer | INSEAD professor, The Culture Map | Books, talks, training | France as principles-first; how to persuade across cultures |
| Geert Hofstede (The Culture Factor) | Dimension scores | Consulting, tool | Country averages, a hint only |
| Michaël Aguilar | Trainer, "Vendeur d'élite" (Dunod), founder of a sales training firm | Training | The French field-sales school (prospecting, meeting setting, a LinkedIn chapter); content not read here |
| Sophie Attia | Author, "Le Social selling" (Dunod, 2017) | Consulting | The French social selling playbook of the late 2010s; not read here |
| Waalaxy (Toinon Georget, co-founder) | French LinkedIn automation tool | Software | Large global datasets with thin method; French templates; tu/vous advice |
| lemlist (Guillaume Moubeche, co-founder) | French cold email and multichannel tool | Software | Personalisation playbooks; no French-language split of its data |
| La Growth Machine | French multichannel tool | Software | Playbooks; its note vs no note test figures could not be traced to a page |
| Overloop (Vincenzo Ruggiero, CEO; acquired by Sortlist) | Belgian prospecting tool, part of an agency marketplace | Software, services | French-language guides; several figures without method, treated as untraced |
| Kaspr | French contact-data extension | Data | A counter-example: fined by the CNIL in 2024 |
| Infopro Digital | French B2B media and events group | Media, events, data | The only recent French B2B buyer journey survey found |
| Intuiti with La Poste Solutions Business | Agency and La Poste's B2B arm | Services | The 2018 to 2020 social selling barometers (650 decision makers) |
| Cognism, Origami, Zeliq, folk | Foreign or French sales tools | Software | Market-entry guides; no data. Cognism's "SDR in France" page now returns 404 |

---

## 10. Examples, written for this folder

All examples are invented, written for this research, and follow the pack's house rules (no recited title, one
reason, one interest question, no dash punctuation). In real output use a non-breaking space before ? and !.

### Good

**1. Traditional industry, plant director, vous.**

> Bonjour Laurent,
> Vous avez commenté le post de votre directeur RSE sur le décret tertiaire : c'est le sujet qui occupe le plus les
> sites industriels avec qui nous travaillons en ce moment. Nous aidons des usines de votre taille à sortir le suivi
> des consommations des tableurs, sans changer les compteurs. Est-ce un chantier ouvert chez vous cette année ?

Why it works: says where the contact came from (the comment), ties it to the reader's job, one fact of substance,
an interest question, vous with first name. About 390 characters.

**2. SaaS founder who posts in tu, tu.**

> Bonjour Inès,
> Ton post sur le passage de 10 à 30 clients m'a parlé, surtout la partie sur les démos qui ne se transforment pas.
> On aide des fondateurs à ce stade à voir quelles démos méritent une relance. Je te montre ce qu'on a vu sur une
> vingtaine de SaaS B2B ? Si ce n'est pas le moment, dis-le-moi, je n'insiste pas.

Why: tu only because she writes in tu publicly; still "Bonjour", no emoji; the offer is something to see, not a
meeting; the easy no is there.

**3. CFO of a mid-size group, vous, principles first.**

> Bonjour Madame Lefèvre,
> Je vous écris parce que les directions financières de groupes multi-entités nous disent toutes la même chose :
> la clôture mensuelle bloque sur les intercos. Nous avons réduit ce délai de quatre jours chez deux groupes de
> distribution. Seriez-vous ouverte à ce que je vous envoie comment ils s'y sont pris ?

Why: the "why you" is a reasoning, not a compliment; one measurable fact (to be true for the user); the ask is to
send something. "Madame + surname" is chosen here for a senior finance reader; "Bonjour Claire," is also fine.

**4. Real estate agency owner, vous, then mirror.**

> Bonjour Karim,
> J'ai vu que votre agence a ouvert un deuxième point de vente à Lyon ce printemps. Beaucoup d'agences à ce moment-là
> nous disent perdre la trace des mandats entre les deux équipes. Est-ce que c'est un sujet chez vous, ou vous avez
> déjà trouvé votre organisation ?

**5. Quebec, operations director, vous.**

> Bonjour Geneviève,
> Votre entrevue sur la pénurie de main-d'oeuvre en entrepôt m'a frappé, surtout le passage sur la formation des
> nouveaux. On aide des centres de distribution québécois à former en deux semaines au lieu de six. Est-ce que ça
> vaudrait la peine que je vous envoie le résumé d'un cas ? Et si vous préférez que je ne vous écrive plus, dites-le-moi.

Note the Quebec vocabulary (entrevue, main-d'oeuvre) and an explicit opt-out line, given CASL.

**6. Swiss private bank, vous, short.**

> Bonjour Monsieur Favre,
> Je vous contacte au sujet de l'archivage des échanges clients, que la FINMA suit de près depuis cette année.
> Nous travaillons avec deux banques privées genevoises sur ce point. Est-ce un sujet sur lequel un retour
> d'expérience vous serait utile ?

(Check any regulatory claim before sending; the example is invented.)

### Bad, and why

| Draft | What is wrong |
|---|---|
| "Salut Marc ! 👋 Ton profil m'a interpellé, je pense qu'on a plein de synergies, tu as 15 min cette semaine ?" | Tu, "Salut" and emoji to a stranger of unknown sector; flattery that proves nothing; "synergies" says nothing; a meeting ask in message one |
| "Bonjour, j'espère que vous allez bien. Je me permets de vous contacter car je suis commercial chez X, leader du marché des solutions innovantes." | No name; two filler openings; talks about the sender; an unprovable superlative |
| "Bonjour Directrice des Achats, Directrice des Achats chez Groupe Y depuis 5 ans." | Recites the title as content; no verb that links a fact to a reason |
| "Hello Sophie, quick question : qui gère la prospection chez vous ?" | English idiom transplanted; asks the reader to do the seller's homework |
| "Bonjour Paul, Vous êtes sans doute très occupé, je serai bref : notre plateforme révolutionnaire augmente vos ventes de 300 %." | Hype and a number nobody believes (uncertainty avoidance); no reason why Paul |
| "Bonjour Jean, ... Dispo pour un call demain ? Tu me dis !" | Mixes vous greeting tone with tu; anglicism "call"; pressure |
| A French message machine-translated from English: "J'espère que ce message vous trouve bien." | Literal translation of "I hope this finds you well"; marks the sender as foreign or automated at once |
| A Belgian reader with a Dutch profile, written in French | Wrong language; check the profile language and location (Flanders, Brussels) |

---

## 11. What the skill should do

1. Persona card field per language: address form (vous / tu / mirror), greeting, sign-off. Default vous with first
   name for every French-speaking market. Allow tu only when the user writes tu and the persona is start-up, tech,
   agency or creative, or when the prospect writes tu publicly.
2. One clause of reason before the ask (principles first). Never a meeting ask in message one.
3. Every French first message carries: who is writing, why this reader in terms of their job, where the contact came
   from if not obvious, and an easy no. This is both the CNIL condition set and good copy.
4. No superlatives or unprovable numbers; one checkable fact at most.
5. French typography in output: space before ? ! : ; and French number formats.
6. Length: 2 to 4 sentences, roughly 300 to 500 characters; never telegraphic fragments.
7. Country checks: Quebec vocabulary and an explicit opt-out; Belgium language check (French or Dutch); Switzerland
   one-to-one only; for any German-speaking Swiss or Belgian reader, switch language and register, never send French.
8. Never quote the untraced numbers in section 6 or rows 16 and 17 of the summary.

## 12. Open questions worth a BeReach measurement

- tu against vous on start-up founders, same template, same sender: the one test nobody has published.
- Whether an explicit easy-no line changes reply rate in French (it is required in spirit; its cost is unknown).
- French against English first messages to French executives in international roles.
